title: Duterte camp wants criminal records of drug war victims
summary: The defense team of former president Rodrigo Duterte has requested access to information pertaining to alleged criminal records of drug war victims and prosecution witnesses participating in the…

blocks.text: November 23, 2026 | 12:00am

Families of victims of extrajudicial killings during the term of former President Rodrigo Duterte air out a sigh of relief while watching a live feed of the appeals chamber of the International Criminal Court (ICC) at the Atencio-Libunao Hall in the University of the Philippines in Diliman, Quezon City as the court rejects the appeal of Duterte to be released and to dismiss his case over jurisdiction on Wednesday, April 22, 2026.
The STAR / Miguel de Guzman

MANILA, Philippines — The defense team of former president Rodrigo Duterte has requested access to information pertaining to alleged criminal records of drug war victims and prosecution witnesses participating in the ongoing proceedings at the International Criminal Court (ICC).

In a 10-page request, defense lawyer Peter Haynes said information on the “criminal antecedents” of some victims and witnesses included in the trial brief submitted by the prosecution should have been part of the material disclosed to them.

Haynes said this is relevant as it is “well-established that the past criminal record or criminal involvement of a witness on whom the prosecution intends to rely at trial can be relevant to assessing their credibility.”

“By way of example, it stands to reason that the defense may seek to use prior criminal convictions involving perjury or false statements to impeach the credibility of a prosecution witness during cross-examination,” read the filing.
“Equally, the requested criminal records of victims may also be exculpatory,” it added.

Haynes noted victims who were subject to arrest warrants, or had faced criminal proceedings, call into question the prosecution’s theory against the operations of the Philippine National Police during the drug war.

“The defense cannot adequately test the prosecution’s case without this material. If the records cast doubt on the prosecution’s case theory, they are relevant to ‘show the innocence of the accused,’” the defense said.

It requested the disclosure of all arrests, convictions, sentences or non-judicial disposals involving witnesses and victims identified in the trial brief, as well as all former or pending arrest warrants and notices issued by the International Criminal Police Organization.

The defense asked the trial chamber to direct the prosecution to immediately seek and obtain information pertaining to these “criminal antecedents,” and disclose those materials to them on or before Nov. 30 for witnesses who will be presented during trial this year.
The prosecution has yet to comment on the matter.
‘Nanlaban’ a lie

Meanwhile, the civil society-led Truth Commission documenting the drug war maintained that the “nanlaban” narrative used by the Duterte administration to explain the killings during police operations was a lie.
In its latest report, the commission said most of the “buy-bust” accounts it documented so far showed that these ended in killings.
Twenty-four of the 46 remains exhumed and examined also showed that they were shot in the head.

The commission said their public registry already identified 8,320 people killed in the “drug war” from 2016 to 2022, describing it as “by far the most definitive count of those who perished” in the campaign.

“The commission’s figure sits between the two numbers most often cited. The government’s most widely used figure, 6,252, counts only suspects killed in operations by the police and the Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency through May 2022,” it said.
“It leaves out people killed by masked gunmen and bodies left on roadsides. The ICC prosecutor has cited 12,000 to 30,000 deaths, drawing on several published sources,” it added.
The commission said its victim registry will be updated once additional information on other victims are verified.
